Triggers.value: Water, flooding, or large bodies of water

Maladaptive Strategies.value: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out
I dwell on how I used to be before the event

Threat.value: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds

Memory.value: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Uniforms): Military or police uniforms
issues.explanation: For a natural-disaster trauma, military/police uniforms are not a plausible primary trigger unless there is additional trauma context; this item points to an interpersonal/authority-related trauma theme not represented elsewhere.

issues.item: Triggers: Name Reminders: Hearing related names
issues.explanation: 'Hearing related names' is hard to reconcile with natural disaster as the index trauma unless a specific deceased/injured person is central, which is not supported by the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: Listening for someone entering the home implies an interpersonal intruder/assailant threat rather than disaster-related danger, creating a cross-node mismatch with the trauma type and trigger/memory content.

issues.item: Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
issues.explanation: Feeling safe only in a very limited number of places can occur in PTSD, but here it clusters with home-intruder monitoring and touch avoidance into an interpersonal-danger profile that is poorly matched to natural disaster trauma.

issues.item: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: The threat item implies fear of an intruder or interpersonal attack in the home, which is hard to reconcile with a natural-disaster trauma profile. With flooding/water triggers present, the expected threat would be environmental danger rather than someone entering the home.

issues.item: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
issues.explanation: Intense shame on recall is not impossible after a natural disaster, but here it lacks support from the rest of the profile: there are no negative-appraisal items about personal blame, humiliation, or moral failure that would make shame a coherent central memory response.

issues.item: Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
issues.explanation: Avoiding all physical contact is more characteristic of interpersonal trauma and is not clinically well linked to the reported disaster-related triggers and memory items. It addresses a symptom domain not otherwise represented in the profile.

vignette:
Elena was fifty-two when Hurricane Isabel tore through her coastal town, and five years later, the storm still felt more present than the past. She remembers the water rising with unnatural speed, a churning, grey mass that swallowed the street, then the yard, then the first floor of her home. The memory itself feels disjointed, like a poorly edited film belonging to someone else. She can recall the sight of her neighbour’s rooftop being submerged and the wrenching grief of knowing Isabel, the woman who had lived there for thirty years, was gone, but she cannot connect these images to her own life. The woman who clung to her own roof rafters for hours, nauseated by the smell of saltwater and gasoline, feels like a stranger.

Her nights are the worst. Elena has come to dread the quiet of her apartment, where every creak of the building or gust of wind sounds like the prelude to disaster. This constant state of high alert means she rarely sleeps for more than an hour or two at a time. Lying awake in the dark, already tense, the sound of a dripping tap can become the relentless advance of floodwater, triggering a cascade of physical sensations. A wave of nausea, identical to the one she felt on the roof, will wash over her, a potent reminder that brings the formless dread of the hurricane rushing back. This feeling of imminent threat has shrunk her world to the four walls of her apartment, the only place she feels a semblance of safety.

The triggers are everywhere. As a physical therapist, she used to find the hydrotherapy pool a place of healing for her patients. Now, the sight of the large body of water makes her stomach clench. When a patient recently mentioned their granddaughter, also named Isabel, Elena was seized by such an intense, image-less wave of grief that she had to excuse herself from the room. These moments, when the full emotional intensity of the trauma returns without a clear picture, are the most terrifying. In response, she has learned to force her mind blank, to stare at a point on the wall and deliberately try to leave her body until the feeling passes. It is this coping mechanism that allows her to function, but it leaves her feeling hollowed out and disconnected. This deliberate dissociation is one of several strategies she has developed; she also finds herself dwelling for hours on the person she used to be—a woman who loved sailing, who wasn't afraid of the rain, who could hear a name without flinching.

This constant retreat, both mental and physical, has created a powerful, self-sustaining cycle. By dwelling on her past self, Elena inadvertently keeps the grief of her loss at the forefront of her mind, ensuring the memory remains raw and painful. Her refusal to go out, born from a need for safety, has made the outside world feel more menacing, sensitizing her to triggers she might otherwise tolerate; the sight of a puddle in the clinic’s parking lot can now feel as threatening as a rising tide. The memory itself seems to generate its own triggers; recalling the event brings back the physical sickness, and that nausea then acts as a fresh catalyst for the memory. The more she tries to escape the feeling through dissociation or avoidance, the more powerful the memory becomes when it inevitably breaks through.

Elena sought therapy after her daughter, visiting from out of state, found her sitting in silence in her darkened living room, unable to go to the grocery store because it had started to rain. Her daughter’s alarm was a mirror to her own despair. Elena confessed that she felt trapped in a loop she couldn't see a way out of. She no longer feels like herself, but like a ghost haunted by a memory that isn't even hers. Her greatest hope is to one day feel the sun on her face without scanning the sky for storm clouds, to hear the name Isabel and remember her friend’s smile instead of the churning grey water.
